summary:
The Space Race is a free, browser-based space mission design game that doubles as a realistic simulator and learning tool. Two players get the same mission and budget, then draft spacecraft parts in real time from one shared, limited pool, so a rival’s choice changes your physics. Players choose a real rocket (Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, New Glenn or Vulcan) plus power, batteries, instruments, antennas and thermal control. After every pick, the game instantly recalculates the real equations mission designers use: rocket equation, launch margin, solar power, radio link, heat balance, battery life and cost. Both spacecraft then fly through today’s live NASA data from JPL Horizons and DONKI. The debrief gives instant feedback on why the mission failed or succeeded, how to fix it, and which real mission faced the same problem. In Rover Expedition mode, players build a rover and drive it in 3D on Mars, the Moon or Venus at real landing sites.

This addresses the challenge by turning real mission design trade-offs into a fun, competitive game. It matters because students learn why spacecraft are built the way they are by deciding, failing, understanding and trying again, which is how real engineers learn.
details:
What it does

The Space Race is a free, browser-based space mission design game that is also a realistic simulator and an interactive learning tool. Two players get the same mission (Mars crater imaging, Venus atmosphere or lunar ice mapping), the same budget and the same live NASA data. They compete to design the spacecraft that returns the most science, alive and under budget. It is not only a game: it teaches real space engineering, with real-time equation calculations and instant feedback on why a mission failed or succeeded.

How it works

  1. Draft: Players pick parts in real time from one shared, limited pool. The parts are a real rocket (Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, New Glenn or Vulcan VC6), propulsion, solar arrays or RTGs, batteries, instruments, data storage, antennas and thermal control. Each part has a real mass, cost, power draw and reliability. Taking the last copy of a part forces the rival onto a heavier or costlier alternative, so your choice changes their physics. Solo players can face an AI rival.
    • Tsiolkovsky rocket equation;
    • thrust-to-weight and launch mass margin (≥15%);
    • inverse-square solar power and radio link;
    • battery depth of discharge and cycle life;
    • heat balance;
    • mission cost.
  2. Launch: The server simulates launch, cruise, orbit insertion and science operations on today’s NASA data: planet positions from JPL Horizons and space weather from NASA DONKI. Each margin becomes a success probability. Both players share the same random seed, so only engineering decides the winner.
  3. Debrief: The game explains why the mission ended the way it did: which equation failed, by how much, how to fix it, and a real mission that hit the same problem, such as JAXA’s Akatsuki engine failure at Venus. Successful missions are explained too.
  4. Rover Expedition: Players build a rover under a $360M cap (chassis, wheels, motors, solar or nuclear power, battery, instruments) and drive it in 3D on Mars, the Moon or Venus. They play at real landing sites at real local solar time, using NASA’s Mars24 algorithm. They must collect samples and send the data home before the battery runs out.

Benefits

  • Players learn by doing: every decision shows its consequence instantly.
  • Every failure becomes a lesson, because the game explains why.
  • Physics challenges earn real in-game budget, so understanding the science is rewarded.
  • Classroom mode gives a whole class the same mission, data and dice, which makes comparison fair.
  • It is free, needs no install, and runs in any browser, including phones with touch controls.

Intended impact

We want students and the public to understand why spacecraft look the way they do. Why mass is everything, why Mars probes need large solar arrays or nuclear power, and why rovers must manage energy carefully. Our goal is to make space mission design accessible to every classroom, especially schools without labs or expensive software, and to inspire future engineers.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite and Three.js for the 3D scenes and rover driving; Web Audio for sound.
  • Backend: Python, Django, Django REST Framework and Django Channels (WebSockets) for real-time drafting and the simulator.
  • Data: PostgreSQL/SQLite and Redis.
  • Hosting: Vercel (frontend) and Render (backend).
  • NASA data: JPL Horizons API, NASA DONKI, Mars24, NASA Planetary Fact Sheets and NASA mission data.

How it is creative

  • The competitive part is the engineering itself. Because the parts pool is shared, your rival’s choice changes your physics. We don’t know of any other game that makes engineering trade-offs competitive.
  • Each match runs on that day’s real NASA data, so a Mars launch really is easier when the real launch window is open.
  • Instant, explained feedback turns a simulator into a teacher.
  • Two modes, orbiter missions and a 3D rover expedition, teach different physics on three worlds.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific accuracy: we validated the model against 21 published numbers, such as Falcon Heavy’s payload to Mars and Curiosity’s RTG output. This testing found and fixed a real bug in our RTG decay model.
  • Fairness: both players get the same mission, NASA snapshot and random seed. Quiz answers are graded on the server.
  • Accessibility: it works in any browser and on mobile, with no install and no cost.
  • Learning design: short matches, clear visual feedback, and an explanation for every result.
  • Honest limitations: some part prices are estimates, thermal is a simplified heat balance, launch windows use Hohmann geometry, and rover terrain is procedurally generated.
